Key Message 1...Mainly dry weather is expected through Saturday.

Cyclonic NW'erly flow aloft and embedded shortwave disturbances
affect Western and Central NY today. At the surface, a weak 
trough continues to impact our region. One trough axis 
accompanying the aforementioned disturbances aloft will sweep 
SE'ward across our CWA during the predawn hours of this morning,
while another will sweep SE'ward across eastern Lake Ontario 
and North-Central NY this afternoon through early evening. 
Isolated showers and thunderstorms are possible along and ahead 
of these surface trough axes prior to sunrise this morning and 
during this afternoon through early evening as low-level 
convergence and moist ascent along the surface trough axes 
release primarily weak boundary layer CAPE amidst moderate to 
strong deep-layer bulk shear. A lack of greater instability 
should prevent storms from becoming severe. Early this evening,
any lingering convection in North-Central NY should dissipate 
by sunset as the boundary layer stabilizes via nocturnal 
cooling. Current odds favor fair weather in Western and Central 
NY tonight through Saturday as a high pressure ridge at the 
surface and aloft builds from the northern Great Plains and 
vicinity, and is accompanied by stabilizing subsidence. However,
a slight chance of a few showers and thunderstorms exists
in/near North-Central NY on Friday, when another shortwave
disturbance embedded in continued NW'erly flow aloft may graze
that portion of our CWA. However, there is disagreement among
various NWP models regarding the amplitude of this shortwave 
trough and whether any associated showers/storms will instead be
focused to the north and east of our CWA.

Weather pattern evolution at the surface and aloft will result 
in negligible air mass change through Saturday. Daily highs in 
the 70's to lower 80's are expected today through Saturday.
Partly to mostly cloudy sky and weak surface winds should be 
accompanied by lows mainly in the 50's to lower 60's around 
daybreak this morning. Clearer sky and weak surface winds should
result in lows reaching mainly the upper 40's to near 60F 
around daybreak Friday and Saturday, respectively. The coolest 
lows are expected in Lewis County, especially the Black River 
Valley, where efficient radiational cooling should be complemented
by cool air drainage from adjacent higher terrain. Note: 
sufficient radiational cooling and low-level moisture should 
result in patchy radiation fog and localized steam fog in the 
valleys of the Western Southern Tier, Finger Lakes, and Eastern 
Lake Ontario Region during the predawn hours through shortly 
after daybreak today through Saturday, respectively.

Key Message 2...The potential for scattered showers and thunderstorms
increases this Saturday night into Sunday.

During Saturday night through Sunday morning, the above-mentioned
ridge at the surface and aloft should exit E'ward and be followed
by W'erly flow aloft and embedded shortwave troughs, in addition
to the NE'ward passage of a surface warm front as a surface low
wobbles E'ward across the northern Great Lakes. The warm front 
will usher-in a warmer and more humid air mass originating over
the Gulf. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of 
the warm front and low-level convergence/moist ascent along the 
surface front should release enough CAPE, including elevated 
CAPE, to generate periodic and scattered showers/thunderstorms. 
Lows should reach the 50's to mid 60's early Sunday morning 
before readings begin to moderate before daybreak as low-level 
WAA strengthens ahead of and behind the surface warm front.

Cyclonic W'erly to WNW'erly flow aloft and embedded shortwave
troughs should impact our region this Sunday afternoon through 
Monday. At the surface, the low may wobble ESE'ward from the 
northern Great Lakes to near the Gulf of Maine, which should 
allow a cold front to sweep E'ward through our CWA Sunday 
evening through Sunday night. Additional scattered showers and 
thunderstorms are expected along and ahead of the cold front, 
amidst weak to perhaps moderate instability and moderate to 
strong deep-layer bulk shear. Severe storms appear possible 
Sunday afternoon into the evening, but their occurrence will be
contingent on multiple factors, including the degree of diurnal
destabilization of the warm/moist sector boundary layer. Behind
the cold front, drier weather is likely Sunday night into 
Monday as a surface ridge attempts to build from the Upper 
Midwest and vicinity. However, isolated rain showers remain 
possible since subtle shortwave troughs aloft and attendant 
surface trough axes should traverse Western and Central NY 
generally from west to east.

High temperatures are forecast to reach the 70's to lower 80's
